subject: Science

unit.unitTitle: What Do Animals and Plants Need to Live?
unit.unitOverview: Assalaamu alaykum, young scientist! Welcome to your first Science unit of Year 2. My name is your AI Tutor, and I will be with you every step of the way. In this unit you are going to become a nature detective. A detective looks closely, asks good questions, and writes down clues. That is exactly what scientists do too.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Science 0846 — Stage 2 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: By the end of this unit, you will be able to do all of the things on this list. Read them now so you know what we are aiming for. At the end you can come back and tick each one when you can do it.
Name the things that all animals need to live: food, water, air, and shelter.
Explain what plants need to live: water, air, light from the Sun, space, and soil for most plants.
Describe different environments such as wet and dry places, sunny and shady places, and say which living things are found there.
Find and name minibeasts like ants, beetles, spiders, worms, and snails, and describe how they help nature.
Give examples of how people can harm the environment (litter and pollution) and how people can protect it.
Observe and record the weather using simple words and charts, and describe how weather affects animals and plants.
Talk about extreme weather such as drought, floods, and dust storms, and explain simple ways to stay safe.
Collect data, tally it, and make a simple bar chart, then read your chart to answer questions.
Use new science words correctly when you speak and write, like habitat, environment, and adaptation.

concepts.title: All Living Things Have Needs
concepts.explanation:
Let us begin with the most important idea of the whole unit. Every living thing has needs. A need is something you must have to stay alive. If you do not get it, you cannot survive. This is true for you, for animals, and for plants.

Think about a young goat, a waxar, on a farm near Baidoa. What does it need every day? It needs food — the fresh grass and leaves it chews. It needs water — a drink from the trough or a puddle. It needs air — the breath it takes in and out without even thinking. And it needs shelter — a shady spot or a pen to keep it safe from the hot sun and from danger. These four needs — food, water, air, and shelter — are the needs of every animal on Earth.

Let us look at each need more closely, one at a time, so you understand it well.

Food is like fuel. When you eat bariis (rice) with a little goat meat, or drink warm camel milk in the morning, your body turns that food into energy. Energy lets you run, play, think, and grow. Animals are the same. A lion eats meat to get its energy. A giraffe stretches its long neck to eat leaves from the tall acacia tree. A little sunbird sips sweet nectar from flowers. Different animals eat different foods, but they all need food to live.

Here is something special about plants. Plants do not eat food the way animals do. Instead, plants make their own food inside their leaves, using sunlight, water, and air. This is one of the most amazing things in all of nature. Because plants can make their own food, they are like the great cooks of the world — and almost every animal depends on the food that plants make.

Water is precious, and in dry lands we know this better than anyone. Every living thing needs water. Your body is mostly made of water, and so is the body of a goat, a beetle, and a blade of grass. Animals drink water to stay alive. A camel is famous because it can go many days without drinking — but even a camel must drink in the end, and it can gulp down a huge amount of water very quickly when it finds a well.

Plants need water too. The roots of the mango tree drink water from the soil and carry it all the way up to the leaves. When the rains come in the Gu season, you can almost see the land turn green as thirsty plants drink deeply. When there is no rain for a long time, the plants dry out and turn brown. This shows us just how important water is.

Air is all around you, even though you cannot see it. Inside the air is a special gas called oxygen. Animals breathe in air to take oxygen into their bodies. You breathe through your nose and mouth. A goat, a lion, and a bird breathe too. Even a fish respires — it uses gills to take in oxygen dissolved in the water.

Plants also use air. They take in a gas from the air called carbon dioxide, and they use it to make their food. Then plants give out oxygen — the very gas that animals and people need to breathe. So plants and animals help each other. This is one of the beautiful ways that Allah has made the living world fit together.

Shelter and space keep living things safe

Every animal needs a safe place — a shelter. Shelter protects an animal from the hot sun, from cold nights, from rain, from strong wind, and from other animals that might harm it. A bird builds a nest. A spider makes a web in a quiet corner. A crab digs a hole in the sand at Lamu beach. A family of goats rests inside a pen at night. Even you have a shelter — your home, where you feel safe and warm.
concepts.example: Plants need space to grow. If plants are squeezed too close together, they must fight for the same sunlight and water, and none of them grow well. That is why a farmer leaves room between the seeds when planting maize or beans. With enough space, each plant can spread its roots and reach the sunlight.

concepts.title: Environments and Habitats
concepts.explanation:
Now that you know what living things need, let us talk about where they live. The place where a living thing makes its home is called its habitat. All the things around it — the air, the soil, the water, the weather, and the other living things — make up its environment.

Not all places are the same. Some places are wet and some are dry. Some places are sunny and some are shady. Some are hot and some are cool. Each kind of place is home to different living things, because different living things need different conditions. Let us take a journey across the land you know and see how the environments change.

Dry places: the savanna and semi-arid land

Much of East Africa is warm and dry, with wide open grasslands called the savanna and drier land called semi-arid land. Here the Sun is strong and rain comes only in certain seasons. The plants that live here are tough. The acacia tree has tiny leaves and sharp thorns to protect its precious water. The baobab tree stores water in its huge, fat trunk. Aloe vera keeps water inside its thick leaves.

The animals here are adapted to the dry land. Camels can walk far to find water and food. Goats nibble on thorny bushes that other animals cannot eat. Giraffes reach the high leaves. Ostriches run fast across the open ground. Every one of these living things is suited to its dry home.

Now imagine a very different place — the edge of the Jubba River, or a green mangrove swamp along the coast. Here there is plenty of water. Frogs and toads live near the water. Fish such as tilapia swim in the river. Dragonflies dart above the surface. Reeds and water plants grow in the soft, wet mud. This wet environment is full of life that could never survive out on the dry savanna.

The coast: the Indian Ocean and coral reefs

Along the Indian Ocean coast, from Mombasa to Kismaayo, there is yet another kind of environment — the sea. Under the waves grow coral reefs, which are like busy underwater cities. Thousands of colourful fish, crabs, sea stars, and other creatures make their homes there. On the sandy beach, tiny crabs scuttle and dig. This salty, watery environment has its own special animals and plants.

Sunny and shady, wet and dry — even at home

You do not have to travel far to find different environments. You can find them in your own home and yard! A sunny windowsill is warm and bright. A shady corner under a table is cool and dim. The ground near a dripping tap is damp, while a shelf indoors is dry. If you look carefully, you will notice that little plants and minibeasts choose different spots. Some like the damp shade, and some like the warm sunshine. Later in this unit you will explore these tiny environments yourself.

Did You Know? A single acacia tree on the savanna can be a habitat for hundreds of creatures at once — ants living in its thorns, birds nesting in its branches, beetles under its bark, and giraffes feeding on its leaves. One tree can be like a whole busy town for living things!
concepts.example: Here is a very important idea: living things are matched to their habitats. A fish is matched to water and would die on dry land. A camel is matched to the dry savanna and would struggle in a wet swamp. When a living thing has special body parts or habits that help it live in its home, we call this an adaptation. A camel's wide feet, an acacia's thorns, and a duck's waterproof feathers are all adaptations. As you explore, keep asking: how is this living thing suited to the place where it lives?

concepts.title: The World of Minibeasts
concepts.explanation:
Now let us shrink down small and meet the minibeasts. A minibeast is a small animal that has no bones inside its body. Insects, spiders, worms, snails, slugs, and centipedes are all minibeasts. They may be tiny, but they are some of the most important animals in the whole world.

You can find minibeasts almost everywhere. Look under a stone and you may find ants and woodlice. Look in the soil and you may find an earthworm. Look on a flower and you may see a butterfly or a bee. Look on a wall in the evening and you may spot a spider waiting quietly in its web. Once you start looking, you will see that minibeasts are all around you.

Scientists sort minibeasts into groups by looking closely at their bodies. Counting legs is a good clue. An insect, such as an ant, a beetle, or a fly, has six legs and often three parts to its body. A spider has eight legs and two body parts, and it is not an insect. A worm has no legs at all and a long soft body. A centipede has many, many legs. When you find a minibeast, count its legs and you will start to know what group it belongs to.

Carries food, lives in a busy nest with many others, works as a team.

Has hard wing covers; the dung beetle rolls animal dung to clean the land.

Drinks nectar from flowers and helps carry pollen from flower to flower.

Spins a web to catch flies; helps keep pests away from the home.

Tunnels through soil, making it soft and healthy for plant roots.

Carries its shell as a shelter; slides slowly on a wet trail.

Some people think minibeasts are just pests to be squashed. But minibeasts do wonderful and important jobs. Bees and butterflies carry pollen from flower to flower. This is called pollination, and it helps plants make fruit and seeds. Without bees, we would have far fewer mangoes, papayas, and beans. Earthworms and beetles break down dead leaves and animal dung, turning them into rich soil that helps new plants grow. Ants clean up tiny scraps of food. And many minibeasts become food for birds, lizards, and frogs. Minibeasts are a small but mighty part of nature.
concepts.example: In Islam, we are taught to be kind to all creatures, even the smallest ones. When you observe a minibeast, be gentle. Look at it carefully, and then let it go back to its home unharmed. A true scientist watches without hurting.

concepts.title: Caring for Our Environment
concepts.explanation:
The earth is a gift, and Allah has made people the khalifah — the carers and guardians of the earth. This means it is our job to look after the land, the water, the plants, and the animals. In this part of the unit you will learn how people can harm the environment, and, more importantly, how we can protect it.

Sometimes people harm nature without meaning to. Litter is rubbish that is dropped on the ground instead of being thrown away properly. A plastic bag blowing across the market in Eastleigh, a bottle left on Lamu beach, or a pile of rubbish by the road can all harm animals. A goat might swallow a plastic bag and become sick. A sea turtle might eat a floating plastic bag, thinking it is a jellyfish.

Pollution is when harmful things get into the air, the water, or the soil. Dirty water can make fish sick and can make people sick too if they drink it. Smoke can dirty the air we breathe. When too many trees are cut down, animals lose the shelter of their habitat, and the soil can blow away. These are the kinds of problems that a good scientist learns to notice and to help solve.

The good news is that everyone, even a young student like you, can help care for the earth. Here are some things you can do:

Do not drop litter. Put your rubbish in a bin, and pick up litter you find (when it is safe and clean to do so).

Reuse and recycle. An old tin can become a plant pot. A jar can be washed and used again instead of thrown away.

Save water. Turn off the tap while you wash, and do not waste this precious gift, especially in the dry season.

Plant and protect trees. Trees give shelter, shade, and clean air, and they hold the soil in place. Planting a mango or acacia tree is a gift to the future.

Be kind to animals. Give water to a thirsty animal, and never harm creatures just for fun.

Keep water clean. Do not throw rubbish into rivers, wells, or the sea.

When you do these things, you are being a good khalifah. You are caring for the world that Allah has trusted to us, and you are helping animals and plants get the things they need to live. Even small good actions add up to make a big difference.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Some communities near the coast plant mangrove trees along the shore. The tangled mangrove roots give baby fish a safe place to grow, protect the land from big waves, and clean the water. Caring for one kind of plant can help many kinds of animals at the same time.

concepts.title: Watching the Weather
concepts.explanation:
Weather is what the air is like at a certain time and place. Is it sunny or cloudy? Is it raining? Is the wind blowing? Is it hot or cool? All of these together are the weather. Weather can change from morning to evening and from day to day.

Weather is very important to living things. When the rains of the Gu season come, the dry land bursts into green, plants grow, and the animals have plenty to eat. In the dry season, the land turns brown and water becomes hard to find. Along the coast, the monsoon winds bring changes to the weather and the sea. People have watched the weather for thousands of years, because it tells them when to plant, when to travel, and when the rains will fill the wells.

Sunny: The Sun shines brightly and the sky is clear. It feels warm or hot.

Cloudy: Grey or white clouds cover the sky and hide the Sun.

Rainy: Water falls from the clouds. Rain gives plants and animals the water they need.

Windy: The air moves and pushes against you. Wind can be a gentle breeze or a strong gust.

Hot and dry: The air is very warm and there is little water. This is common in the dry season.
concepts.example: A real weather scientist is called a meteorologist. You can be one too! Each day, look outside and describe the weather. Is it sunny, cloudy, rainy, or windy? Is it hot or cool? Write it down in a weather chart. If you do this every day for a week or two, you will have a set of data. Then you can look at your data and notice patterns — for example, you might see that most days that week were sunny, or that the wind blew hardest in the afternoon. Noticing patterns is what scientists love to do.

concepts.title: Extreme Weather and Staying Safe
concepts.explanation:
Most days the weather is ordinary. But sometimes the weather becomes extreme, which means very strong or unusual. Extreme weather can be dangerous for people, animals, and plants. Learning about it helps us stay safe and helps us care for living things when hard times come.

A drought happens when there is no rain for a very long time. The land dries up, the grass dies, wells and rivers shrink, and animals struggle to find water and food. Droughts are a serious problem in dry lands. During a drought, people share water, give water to their animals, and sometimes move their herds to find greener land. Drought reminds us how precious every drop of water is.

A flood is the opposite of a drought. It happens when so much rain falls that the rivers, like the Jubba, overflow and cover the land with water. Floods can wash away homes and crops. If there is ever a flood near you, the safest thing is to move to higher ground with your family and stay away from fast-moving water.
concepts.example: In dry places, strong winds can pick up sand and dust and carry it in a thick cloud called a dust storm. Dust storms make it hard to see and hard to breathe. If a dust storm comes, go indoors, close the windows, and cover your nose and mouth with a cloth. Near the ocean, very strong storms can bring powerful winds and huge waves.

methods.title: What Do Seeds Need to Grow?
methods.example: To find out whether seeds need water and light to grow well. Your Hypothesis Before you start, write down what you think will happen. Which seeds do you think will grow best — the ones with water and light, or the ones without? Guessing first is what real scientists do. Your guess is called a hypothesis.
steps: Put a little damp cotton wool or soil in each of the 3 cups.
Place 2 or 3 bean seeds in each cup.
Cup A: give water and put it on a sunny windowsill.
Cup B: give water but put it in a dark cupboard.
Cup C: give NO water and put it on the sunny windowsill.

methods.title: A Minibeast Hunt and Count
methods.example: To find out which minibeasts live near your home, and which one is the most common. Your Hypothesis Which minibeast do you think you will see the most? Ants? Beetles? Write your guess before you begin.
steps: Choose a safe spot outdoors — a corner of the yard, near a wall, or under a stone or leaf.
Look quietly for 10 minutes. Move slowly so you do not scare the minibeasts.
Each time you see a minibeast, make a tally mark next to its name in your table.
Gently look at one or two closely in your clear jar, then let them go back where you found them.
Count how many legs each one has to help you name it.

methods.title: Build a Weather Station
methods.example: To observe and record the weather for one week, like a real meteorologist. Your Hypothesis What kind of weather do you think will happen most this week? Sunny? Cloudy? Write your guess.
steps: Set your rain jar outside in an open spot, away from walls and trees.
Tie your wind flag to a stick and push it into the ground where the wind can reach it.
At the same time each day (for example, after fajr or midday), look at the sky and your tools.
Write down: Is it sunny, cloudy, or rainy? Is it windy or still? Is it hot or cool? Is there any rain in the jar?
Do this every day for one week.

methods.title: Comparing Wet and Dry Homes
methods.example: To compare a damp, shady place and a dry, sunny place, and see which living things like each one. Your Hypothesis Do you think more little living things will be found in the damp shady place or the dry sunny place? Write your guess.
steps: Choose your two places: one damp and shady, one dry and sunny.
Look carefully at the first place for 5 minutes. Write down every plant and minibeast you can see.
Feel the ground gently (then wash your hands). Is it damp or dry? Is the air cool or warm?
Do exactly the same at the second place.
Compare your two lists.

workedExamples.title: Counting and Charting Minibeasts
workedExamples.prompt: Let us work through an example together, step by step, just like a real scientist would. Imagine that Amina went into her yard in Hargeisa with a notebook. She wanted to find out which minibeast was the most common. Here is exactly what she did.
workedExamples.solution:
Step 1 — Ask a question. Amina asked: Which minibeast will I see most in my yard in ten minutes?

Step 2 — Make a plan. She decided to watch for ten minutes and make a tally mark for every minibeast she saw.

Step 3 — Collect the data. She saw 6 ants, 3 beetles, 2 butterflies, and 1 spider. She made a tally mark for each one as she saw it.

Step 4 — Count the tallies. Ants: 6. Beetles: 3. Butterflies: 2. Spider: 1. In total she saw 12 minibeasts.

activities.title: What Do Seeds Need to Grow?
activities.materials: A few bean seeds or maize seeds (dried beans from the kitchen work well); 3 small cups, tins, or cut-open plastic bottles; Cotton wool, or a little soil; Water; A sunny windowsill and a dark cupboard
steps: Put a little damp cotton wool or soil in each of the 3 cups.
Place 2 or 3 bean seeds in each cup.
Cup A: give water and put it on a sunny windowsill.
Cup B: give water but put it in a dark cupboard.
Cup C: give NO water and put it on the sunny windowsill.

activities.title: A Minibeast Hunt and Count
activities.materials: A notebook and pencil; An old clear jar or cup (to look closely, then release the minibeast); A magnifying glass if you have one (a drop of water on clear plastic also magnifies); A soft spoon or leaf to gently lift a minibeast
steps: Choose a safe spot outdoors — a corner of the yard, near a wall, or under a stone or leaf.
Look quietly for 10 minutes. Move slowly so you do not scare the minibeasts.
Each time you see a minibeast, make a tally mark next to its name in your table.
Gently look at one or two closely in your clear jar, then let them go back where you found them.
Count how many legs each one has to help you name it.

activities.title: Build a Weather Station
activities.materials: A notebook or a chart you draw yourself; An empty clear bottle or jar to catch rain (a simple rain gauge); A strip of cloth or a light plastic bag tied to a stick (a wind flag); Your own eyes to watch the sky
steps: Set your rain jar outside in an open spot, away from walls and trees.
Tie your wind flag to a stick and push it into the ground where the wind can reach it.
At the same time each day (for example, after fajr or midday), look at the sky and your tools.
Write down: Is it sunny, cloudy, or rainy? Is it windy or still? Is it hot or cool? Is there any rain in the jar?
Do this every day for one week.
Safety: Plastic bags are not toys — never put them over or near your face.

activities.title: Comparing Wet and Dry Homes
activities.materials: Your notebook and pencil; A magnifying glass if you have one; Two places to compare: a damp, shady spot (near a tap or under a plant) and a dry, sunny spot
steps: Choose your two places: one damp and shady, one dry and sunny.
Look carefully at the first place for 5 minutes. Write down every plant and minibeast you can see.
Feel the ground gently (then wash your hands). Is it damp or dry? Is the air cool or warm?
Do exactly the same at the second place.
Compare your two lists.

activities.title: Observe: Watching the Weather
activities.materials: A few bean seeds or maize seeds (dried beans from the kitchen work well); 3 small cups, tins, or cut-open plastic bottles; Cotton wool, or a little soil; Water; A sunny windowsill and a dark cupboard
steps: Look for an example of watching the weather around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Living thing and Environment.
Explain your finding out loud, as if you were teaching it. Say it to a family member or your teacher if someone is nearby, or explain it to yourself and check it against the concept explanations.

activities.title: Sort: Extreme Weather and Staying Safe
activities.materials: A notebook and pencil; An old clear jar or cup (to look closely, then release the minibeast); A magnifying glass if you have one (a drop of water on clear plastic also magnifies); A soft spoon or leaf to gently lift a minibeast
steps: Look for an example of extreme weather and staying safe around your home or outside.

rules.title: Key idea 1
rules.text: All animals need FOUR things to live: food, water, air, and shelter. Plants need water, air, light from the Sun, and space — and most plants also need soil. A good way to remember animal needs is to picture your favourite animal and ask: does it have food, water, air, and a safe home?

rules.title: Key idea 2
rules.text: In extreme weather, the most important thing is to stay safe with your family and a trusted adult. Drought means too little rain. Flood means too much rain. In a flood, move to higher ground. In a dust storm, go indoors and cover your nose and mouth.

terms: Living thing
Something that is alive; it grows, needs food and water, and can make more of itself.
Environment
All the things around a living thing: air, water, soil, weather, and other living things.
Habitat
The home where a plant or animal lives and finds everything it needs.
Needs
Things a living thing must have to stay alive.
Shelter
A safe place where an animal rests and is protected from weather and danger.
Minibeast
A small animal with no bones, such as an insect, spider, worm, or snail.
Insect
A minibeast with 6 legs, like an ant, beetle, or butterfly.
Adaptation
A special body part or habit that helps a living thing survive where it lives.
Pollution
Harmful things people put into the air, water, or land.
Weather
What the air is like today: sunny, cloudy, rainy, windy, hot, or cool.
Drought
A long time with too little rain.
Flood
When too much rain covers the land with water.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name the four things that all animals need to live.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Food, water, air, and shelter. Explanation: These four needs are true for every animal, from an ant to an elephant.
Plants need water to stay alive, to grow, and to help make their own food. Explanation: Roots drink water from the soil and carry it up to the leaves.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between an insect and a spider?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: An insect has 6 legs and a spider has 8 legs. Explanation: Counting legs is the quickest way to tell them apart; a spider is not an insect.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name two helpful jobs that minibeasts do in nature.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Any two of: carrying pollen between flowers (pollination), breaking down dead leaves and dung to make soil, cleaning up scraps, and being food for other animals. Explanation: Minibeasts do small but very important jobs.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Give one example of how people can harm the environment.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Any one of: dropping litter, polluting water or air, or cutting down too many trees. Explanation: These actions take away the things animals and plants need.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Give one example of how you can protect the environment.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Any one of: not dropping litter, saving water, reusing and recycling, planting trees, or being kind to animals. Explanation: Small good actions help care for the earth.

selfAssessment: I can by the end of this unit, you will be able to do all of the things on this list. Read them now so you know what we are aiming for. At the end you can come back and tick each one when you can do it.
I can name the things that all animals need to live: food, water, air, and shelter.
I can explain what plants need to live: water, air, light from the Sun, space, and soil for most plants.
I can describe different environments such as wet and dry places, sunny and shady places, and say which living things are found there.
I can find and name minibeasts like ants, beetles, spiders, worms, and snails, and describe how they help nature.
I can give examples of how people can harm the environment (litter and pollution) and how people can protect it.
I can observe and record the weather using simple words and charts, and describe how weather affects animals and plants.
I can talk about extreme weather such as drought, floods, and dust storms, and explain simple ways to stay safe.
